Block Party | Civic Tech Mobile App

Reimagining civic participation through interactive urban design

A gamified mobile experience that empowers residents to visualize neighborhood changes, propose ideas, and shape the future of their communities.

Overview

Bloomington’s public input process for urban planning projects relied on newsletters, surveys, and council meetings, yet many younger residents were unaware of opportunities to participate. Research with residents and city planners led me to focus on civic-oriented residents aged 18–35 and make urban proposals easier to understand and respond to.

Working with the City Council of Bloomington, Indiana, I developed Block Party, an interactive community planning mobile app. Its visual planning sandbox lets residents arrange predefined features such as parks and bike lanes, create proposals, vote, and share feedback—making neighborhood planning more accessible.

Key Impact

42% increase in community engagement

Beta testing with 30 Bloomington residents showed higher participation through proposal submissions, with a reported 42% increase in engagement compared with previous participation patterns.

The Problem

A proposal cannot invite input if people cannot picture it.

Bloomington’s existing input channels included newsletters, surveys, council meetings, and design presentations. Research exposed gaps in awareness, convenience, and visual context. I narrowed a broad urban-design ambition to community projects and civic-oriented residents aged 18–35.

How might we help younger residents understand neighborhood changes and contribute ideas that planners can interpret?

Documented Findings → Design Implications
EvidenceDesign implication
Low awareness and inconvenient participation.Let residents explore projects beyond a meeting.
Proposals shown without enough spatial context.Locate a proposed change in its neighborhood.
Feedback could be misinterpreted.Pair comments with visual ideas and project context.

Concept Evaluation

Keep the context of a place. Add the freedom to propose.

A co-design workshop with four participants explored three directions. After designing and evaluating paper concepts with two city planners and two users, I developed a visual planning sandbox: contextual feedback plus a way to arrange and share ideas.

Explored · Kiosk

Build together, in person.

Collaborative blocks at City Hall offered shared discussion, tied to organized sessions.

Explored · AR

Overlay a proposal on a place.

An AR concept connected feedback to a resident’s view of the physical site.

Selected · Visual planning sandbox

Explore, respond, and create.

A virtual neighborhood combined proposal feedback with resident-built ideas in one experience.

Testing & Iterations

Testing made choice and feedback the next priorities.

Six Bloomington residents tested the 2025 high-fidelity prototype. Their feedback identified two refinements. The later mobile app carries these refinements into the participation flow.

Choosing an element
2025 findingPrefab elements needed clearer organization.
Later changeBuildings, Outdoors, and Mobility categories give the library structure.
Recognizing a result
2025 findingA new design’s arrival in the plot needed emphasis.
Later changePlacement feedback and a submission preview show the result of an action.

Final Solution

Explore, propose, and follow what happens next.

Block Party demonstrates three connected participation flows: understand a project, create a proposal in a visual planning sandbox, and follow updates. Residents arrange predefined assets and share ideas through a visual, game-like experience. Beta testing with 30 Bloomington residents showed a reported 42% increase in community engagement through proposal submissions.

01 · Understand a project

Explore → Hopewell West → expand the sheet. Read context before contributing.

02 · Put an idea in place

Design this space → choose or drag an element → Review idea. A limited library reduces the blank-page task.

03 · Stay involved

Notifications → My proposals. A reference, next step, and review stage explain what follows.

The Impact

42% increase in community engagement.

42%Increase in community engagement · Beta testing

Streamlining public input.

In beta testing with 30 Bloomington residents, proposal submissions reflected a reported 42% increase in community engagement compared with previous participation patterns. The visual planning sandbox gave residents a more approachable way to contribute ideas.

Six Bloomington residents tested the 2025 prototype, saw potential for inclusive engagement, and identified two usability refinements. The beta findings are distinct from this earlier usability study.

Reflections

A digital channel needs a representative conversation.

Architecture taught me that a proposal changes everyday life. This project taught me to narrow the question enough to test it—and to consider whose input reaches a decision.

Ready-made elements lower the barrier to proposing, while limiting what residents can express. Next, I would test the revised builder and feedback flow across different levels of digital confidence, then work with planners on interpreting conflicting input. Outreach and a credible review process need to grow alongside the interface.
